claims.text: The initial FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA is an ordered, single-phase hexagonal material.
Such FeMnNiGeSi-type HEAs are typically produced as arc-melted ingots or melt-spun ribbons.
The initial material has relatively large grains and limited surface area.
The controlled intervention is approximately 5 hours of high-energy ball milling under argon followed by consolidation below 500 degrees Celsius.
Ball milling produces grain refinement and a higher density of grain boundaries.
The proposed processing produces nanocrystalline domains.
Sintering below 500 degrees Celsius will preserve the ordered hexagonal phase and prevent substantial grain growth.
Grain boundaries and nanocrystalline domains act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for the magnetostructural transition.
Increasing grain-boundary density reduces the nucleation-energy barrier for the magnetostructural phase change.
The reduced nucleation barrier makes the magnetostructural transition broader, more gradual, and more reversible.
The refined microstructure decreases hysteretic losses during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Milling followed by consolidation increases the effective surface-to-volume ratio and therefore improves heat-exchange rates.
Relative to the baseline, the processed sample will retain a comparable peak magnetic-entropy change.
Relative to the baseline, the processed sample will show improved cycling reversibility and faster heat-exchange kinetics.
The baseline alloy has a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition with a large but hysteretic entropy change.
The predicted improvements require retention of the single-phase ordered structure and sufficient refinement without unwanted phase transformations.
The predicted effects are limited to temperatures near the magnetic transition under low-applied-field cycling.
Failure to reduce hysteretic losses or broaden the transition relative to the baseline would falsify the grain-boundary-mediated hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The material is repeatedly called 'as-deposited,' but arc-melted ingots are not deposited materials and melt-spun ribbons are normally described as rapidly solidified rather than as-deposited.

The intervention consolidates powder into a sintered body, while the mechanism assumes an increased surface-to-volume ratio and faster heat exchange without specifying retained porosity, particle geometry, or another reason consolidation would preserve a larger effective surface area.
